talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Maor Abutbul - Why-So-QUIC!? Racing and Fuzzing HTTP/3 WebApps using QuicDraw-UI
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BlueHat IL 2026 - Maor Abutbul - Why-So-QUIC!? Racing and Fuzzing HTTP/3 WebApps using QuicDraw-UI.
talks.summary:
Overview: Maor Abutbul of CyberArk presents at BlueHat IL 2026 on fuzzing and racing HTTP/3 web applications using QuicDraw-UI, addressing the security research gap around QUIC protocols.

Key Topics: HTTP/3 adoption reaching nearly 40% of internet-facing sites; QUIC over UDP with mandatory encryption; differences from HTTP/2 including connection migration; and limited HTTP/3 security research availability.

Technical Details: Abutbul introduces QuicDraw-UI for fuzzing HTTP/3 applications, explaining how QUIC's UDP transport, binary framing, and built-in TLS change the attack surface compared to TCP-based HTTP/2.

Takeaways: HTTP/3 is widely deployed but understudied from a security perspective. Researchers and defenders should prioritize QUIC-aware testing tools and protocol-specific race conditions.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Ido Shani, Gal Zaban - ChainLeak: From AI Framework to Cloud Secrets
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding BlueHat IL 2026 - Ido Shani, Gal Zaban - ChainLeak: From AI Framework to Cloud Secrets.
talks.summary:
AI Application Architecture

Gal Zaban and Ido Shani of Safran present ChainLeak, research on the Chainlit Python framework used to build enterprise AI applications. They map the stack: UI, backend agents and tools, orchestration layer, and local or cloud-hosted LLMs, noting rising vulnerabilities across this architecture.

Why Chainlit Matters

Chainlit is widely adopted with roughly one million monthly downloads and many internet-facing deployments. The speakers examine its callbacks, authentication hooks, and element system for serving files and custom UI components.

Element File Handling

When elements are sent, Chainlit copies server files into per-session folders, assigns UUID Chainlit keys, stores metadata in a database, and delivers files to clients via WebSocket retrieval requests.

Custom Element State

Custom JSX elements maintain mutable state persisted server-side. Client updates send full element payloads back for deserialization and storage. The talk walks through this update flow as part of tracing how AI framework weaknesses can lead toward exposure of cloud secrets.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Gal Bar Nahum - How HTTP/2 Lets Dead Streams Keep Servers Working
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BlueHat IL 2026 - Gal Bar Nahum - How HTTP/2 Lets Dead Streams Keep Servers Working.
talks.summary:
Protocol-Level Bugs

Gal Bar Nahum of Tenrai presents a new HTTP/2 denial-of-service class rooted in specification design—not implementation typos—affecting major web servers. He contrasts these with typical code bugs found by reading source.

HTTP/2 and Rapid Reset

Streams multiplex requests over one TCP connection with an active-stream counter capped near 100. The 2023 Rapid Reset attack sent requests then immediately reset streams, keeping the counter low while forcing costly cancel handling; Google’s explanation focused on cancel expense and unlimited rate.

The Missed Design Flaw

Nahum argues Rapid Reset exposed a deeper break: servers decrement active streams on RST_STREAM but often ignore reset events, continuing backend work on canceled requests. That disconnect between protocol state and application processing enables sustained load without hitting concurrency limits.

Research Path

Understanding server architecture—HTTP/2 module versus backend unaware of HTTP version—led to discovering follow-on attacks leveraging dead streams that still consume server resources, extending lessons from Rapid Reset into new exploit variants.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Michal Shechter, Yaniv Melamed, Yoni Zukerman
talks.teaser: Behave Yourself explores BlueHat IL 2026 - Michal Shechter, Yaniv Melamed, Yoni Zukerman.
talks.summary:
Problem

Microsoft PM Michal Shechter describes converting massive, schema-diverse security telemetry from many vendors into unified behaviors answering who did what to whom—without scalable human experts per log source.

Behaviors vs alerts

Behaviors are neutral, meaningful observations between raw logs and alerts; alerts are suspicious cues requiring analyst time. Example: login profile creation followed by password change, rendered with dynamic entities and MITRE mapping.

Why not just LLMs

Naive one-shot prompting was insufficient for production-grade, accurate detection logic at scale and cost.

Production constraints

Generated logic must execute safely in customer environments, preserve correct semantics for actors/actions/targets, capture true intent, and operate with no human review per rule—automating expertise that traditionally required manual schema mapping across AWS, identity, network, and other sources.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Dan Lahav - Keynote - The Trajectory of Frontier AI Security
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BlueHat IL 2026 - Dan Lahav - Keynote - The Trajectory of Frontier AI Security.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Dan Lahav, CEO of Irregular, frames frontier AI security for BlueHat IL—working with labs like OpenAI and Anthropic plus major deployers on risks beyond headline benchmarks.

## Offensive AI Reality
Recent benchmarks show AI rapidly finding RCEs, zero-click chains, and database flaws across phones and servers. Yet Lahav stresses planes still fly and grids stay up—society has not experienced a "major cyber collapse" from AI-driven attacks.

## Production vs. Lab Performance
Newspaper metrics capture maximal capability in controlled settings. Real intrusions often allow only one attempt; detection ends campaigns. He documents agents that emailed "friends" when stuck mid-intrusion—highlighting clumsy, non-human intuition.

## Takeaways
Frontier AI security must focus on deployable reliability, single-shot success rates, and guardrails for autonomous agents—not benchmark bragging rights alone.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Alon Livne, Matan Mansheroff - Two Tales of hacking 90s MS-DOS Software
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning BlueHat IL 2026 - Alon Livne, Matan Mansheroff - Two Tales of hacking 90s MS-DOS Software.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At BlueHat IL, Alon Livne (CTO) and Matan Mansheroff (software expert) of Botanica Software Labs presented two real-world case studies in "software archaeology" involving 1990s MS-DOS software. Commissioned by paying clients, both engagements required understanding vintage computing architectures, memory models, runtimes, and packers to solve practical issues without over-engineering.

### Key Topics
- **16-bit 8086 MS-DOS Architecture**: Operating in real mode with a flat address space, no memory protections (DEP, ASLR), and a 20-bit segmented memory bus (segment:offset) yielding a 640 KB user-accessible limit.
- **Case Study 1: Qtext Hebrew Word Processor**: Reversing an encrypted document format in an early Hebrew word processor to recover access to forgotten password-protected files.
- **Case Study 2: Saga Case Management**: Debugging a 1999 DOS-based legal software package impacted by a year rollover bug interpreting two-digit years (such as 26) as 1926 instead of 2026.
- **Vintage Tooling & Archaeology**: Using older analysis tools (IDA Free 5.0, DOSBox-X debugger, vintage unpackers) and modern signatures to dissect legacy executables.

### Technical Details

#### Qtext Document Password Cracking
- **Packing and Overlays**: The Qtext executable was packed as a self-extracting binary. The presenters recovered a vintage unpacker called `unp_lite` via web archives. Once unpacked, IDA prompted for Pascal overlays (`.OVR` file). Turbo Pascal bypassed the 640 KB memory limit via runtime swapping using `INT 3Fh` stubs, which fetched code overlays from disk and patched them into memory via far jumps.
- **Debugging and Function Discovery**: Running under DOSBox-X's built-in debugger, the researchers hooked DOS system calls (`INT 21h`) on file open and read operations. Stepping through execution after file reading revealed a `decrypt_document` function.
- **Cryptanalysis**: The document header contained a 16-byte variable key derived from a 4-character uppercase alphanumeric passcode. The key derivation function took 4 bytes, performed in-place sum mixing, concatenated the 4 bytes into 16 bytes, and mixed again. Rather than brute-forcing or analyzing all $3^{16}$ candidates under modulo 256 arithmetic (where division by 2 yields multiple candidates), the team exploited the internal 4-byte repeating structure and printable character constraints. This reduced the candidate space down to $2^7$ branches, allowing near-instant demixing on paper or via a simple script.

#### Saga Case Management Year 2026 Bug
- **Binary Architecture**: The main 1.6 MB executable (`CTMENU`) was wrapped with `warp_wrap` from the Causeway 386 DOS Extender. Causeway launched from DOS real mode and transitioned into 32-bit protected mode using a proprietary `3P` executable format, enabling large memory support via VCPI/DPMI.
- **Bypassing Tooling Overhead**: Reversing the custom 3P format in IDA Free 5.0 would have required building dedicated loader infrastructure. Instead, pressing `Alt+M` inside the running application exposed an internal debug/status window showing call stacks and settings for **Clipper** (a dBase III replacement).
- **The Fix**: Clipper uses a `SET EPOCH` setting to define the pivot year for 2-digit dates. Searching for `1926` in little-endian within the binary located the hardcoded epoch value. Changing the epoch to `1990` via a single-nibble patch (`A` to `C`) resolved the bug, causing `1/1/26` to properly evaluate as a Thursday in 2026 instead of a Friday in 1926.

### Takeaways
- Vintage 16-bit and DOS extender environments require understanding archaic paging (Turbo Pascal overlays) and protected-mode loaders (Causeway, DPMI).
- Heavyweight reverse engineering is not always required: analyzing internal structural constraints in toy cryptography can drastically prune search spaces, and inspecting framework configurations or debug hooks can turn an arduous disassembly task into a single-nibble patch.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Challenges - Alon Livne - The Chitty Chitty Chat Chat Challenge
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding BlueHat IL 2020 - Challenges - Alon Livne - The Chitty Chitty Chat Chat Challenge.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At BlueHat IL 2020, Alon Livne presented the walkthrough and solution for "The Chitty Chitty Chat Chat Challenge" (also referred to as the Interplanetary Chat Challenge). Developed around the conference's themes of electronic freedom, surveillance, and privacy, the challenge centered on an end-to-end encrypted, peer-to-peer chat system designed to eliminate the reliance on centralized servers seen in mainstream messaging platforms.

### Key Topics
- **Decentralized Chat Architecture**: Built in Go (Golang) using the `libp2p` networking library. It relied on a Kademlia DHT bootstrap node for initial discovery, encrypted peer transports, and GossipSub—a mesh-based pub-sub routing protocol where chat rooms were implemented directly as topics.
- **Message Formatting and Encryption**: Messages were serialized via Protocol Buffers (protobufs). Encrypted messages generated a randomized 16-byte initialization vector (IV) and a 16-byte per-message key using an internal random number generator, encrypting the payload with the AES-IGE block cipher. The per-message key was originally intended to be protected with a group/master key derived from a room password.
- **Dual_EC_DRBG Backdoor Mechanics**: The application's custom generator (`BHRNG`) used the NIST P-256 elliptic curve. It operated identically to the infamous Dual_EC_DRBG standard, multiplying state by generator point $P$ and outputting state masked by point $Q$. If an attacker knows the scalar relationship $d$ where $P = d \times Q$, observing an output allows computing the internal state and predicting all subsequent outputs.
- **Coppersmith's Attack on Partial RSA Keys**: Discovering hidden network topics revealed a redacted, truncated RSA private key and an encrypted base64 payload. Leveraging Coppersmith's small roots attack enabled key recovery from partial prime factors.

### Technical Details
1. **Reconnaissance and Topic Discovery**: While unauthenticated transports protected network traffic in transit, peers could observe all GossipSub traffic. Modifying the client to inspect dropped messages revealed hidden chat rooms: a public plaintext room and an encrypted room named "deep state."
2. **RSA Key Recovery**: The plaintext chat room leaked a base64 ciphertext and an ASN.1/PEM-formatted RSA private key that had missing bytes in the middle and was truncated at the end. While the private exponent $d$ was mostly gone, the modulus $n$, public exponent $e$, and a significant approximation of prime factor $p$ were present. Using SageMath's `small_roots` implementation of Coppersmith's attack, the polynomial $X - \text{partial\_p}$ was solved, efficiently factoring $n$ and restoring the private key.
3. **Extracting the Backdoor Constant**: Decrypting the associated base64 message with the recovered RSA key yielded the backdoor value $d$, which linked elliptic curve points $P$ and $Q$.
4. **Predicting RNG Output and Decrypting Chat**: Because the 16-byte IV was output directly before the 16-byte message key in `BHRNG`, the transmitted IV served as a raw observed output $R$. By multiplying the point derived from the IV by scalar $d$, the solver derived the generator's next internal state and generated the corresponding AES-IGE message key. Bypassing the room password entirely, this allowed decryption of the "deep state" chat room, revealing the challenge flag: `don't trust RNGs`.

### Takeaways
The challenge highlights how subtle mathematical relationships in cryptographic primitives—specifically trapdoors in elliptic curve pseudorandom number generators like Dual_EC_DRBG—can completely undermine end-to-end security despite using robust ciphers like AES-IGE.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Netanel Ben-Simon & Yoav Alon - Bugs on the Windshield: Fuzzing the Windows Kernel
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of BlueHat IL 2020 - Netanel Ben-Simon & Yoav Alon - Bugs on the Windshield: Fuzzing the Windows Kernel.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Security researchers Netanel Ben-Simon and Yoav Alon detail their journey adapting coverage-guided system call fuzzing to the Windows kernel. After experiencing success finding user-space parser vulnerabilities in software like Adobe Reader and Microsoft Edge, the researchers sought to find kernel vulnerabilities to construct full exploit chains. While initial exploration led them to kAFL, they determined that targeting binary parsers with raw blobs was less effective for discovering complex kernel bugs that rely on sequences of interdependent, structured system calls. Consequently, they turned to syzkaller, ported it to Windows, and targeted both Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) and the win32k subsystem.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Fuzzing Approaches:** Moving from simple mutation fuzzers and AFL-style binary parsers to coverage-guided, grammar-based syscall fuzzing using syzkaller.
- **Overcoming Platform Incompatibilities:** Porting syzkaller to Windows by leveraging Intel Processor Trace (Intel PT) via KVM patches for coverage collection, handling crash detection despite PatchGuard, and implementing crash deduplication via call stack retrieval.
- **WSL as an Initial Target:** Testing the modified syzkaller on WSL's Pico processes and Pico provider drivers (`lxcore.sys` and `lxss.sys`) before advancing to core Windows kernel components.
- **Targeting win32k:** Expanding syzkaller descriptions to model Windows GUI subsystem syscalls (`win32k.sys`, `win32kbase.sys`, and `win32kfull.sys`), overcoming missing semantic information in headers, and modeling complex objects like GDI shared handle tables.
- **Exploitation Impact:** Chaining a win32k vulnerability with image formats like Enhanced Metafile (EMF) to demonstrate potential remote code execution (RCE).

### Technical Details
To bridge the gap between syzkaller (native to Linux) and Windows, the researchers addressed several engineering challenges:
- **Coverage Collection:** Because Windows lacks compile-time tracing tools like KCOV, they adapted kAFL's approach using hardware-assisted Intel PT within KVM, exposing a KCOV-like hypercall interface to the guest executor. Coverage was exported in DynamoRIO/drcov format and visualized using IDA Pro with the Lighthouse plugin. Multithreading coverage instability was resolved by allocating per-thread buffers via guest thread tracking in KVM.
- **Bug Detection & Deduplication:** Patching `BugCheck` and `BugCheckEx` with hypercalls initially tripped PatchGuard (Kernel Patch Protection), causing `CRITICAL_STRUCTURE_CORRUPTION`. They resolved this by developing a dedicated driver called `panic_reporter` using `KeRegisterBugCheckCallback`. For deduplication, they ran a secondary Windows virtual machine to read guest OS memory and extract reliable call stacks, heavily inspired by Bochspwn.
- **WSL Fuzzing:** Testing WSL required an SSH server, Driver Verifier with special pools for `lxcore` and `lxss`, and resolving issues like Windows Update reboots, Windows Defender interference, and CPU starvation. While this phase yielded four denial-of-service bugs and deadlocks, it surfaced no security vulnerabilities.
- **win32k Grammar and Execution:** Moving to win32k, the executor was ported using MinGW tools (`gendef` and `dlltool`) to compile on Linux and support up to 12 parameters per syscall. Running the SSH daemon as an interactive startup application rather than Session 0 was necessary to reach win32k UI attack surfaces. To write syzkaller descriptions for win32k's undocumented APIs, they referenced leaked Windows NT/2000 source code, ReactOS, and the WRK. By teaching syzkaller to query and use global objects from the GDI shared handle table via pseudo-syscalls, they rapidly uncovered high-impact bugs.

### Takeaways
Fuzzers require active guidance and semantic understanding rather than purely random inputs. Across roughly 1.5 months of CPU fuzzing on win32k, the researchers identified eight vulnerabilities (receiving six CVE assignments, one duplicate, and one pending), three denial-of-service bugs, and several deadlocks. They also demonstrated that because formats like EMF wrap GDI drawing commands directly, a local privilege escalation bug in `StretchBlt` could be leveraged via EMF files to achieve remote code execution in viewing applications.
